## Proof

**Claim:** The inequality $BAB \le A$ in the quadratic-form (Loewner) sense does **not** hold in general, even when $A$ and $B$ are entrywise non-negative and $0 \le B \le 1$.

**Counterexample.** Take

$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

Both matrices are entrywise non-negative, and every entry of $B$ lies in $[0,1]$, so $0 \le B \le 1$ entrywise. Moreover $A$ is positive semidefinite (it equals $u u^{\mathsf T}$ with $u=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}$), and $B$ is an orthogonal projection, so $0 \le B \le I$ holds even in the operator sense. Thus this example is valid under either interpretation of "$0 \le B \le 1$."

Compute $BAB$:

$$
BA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
$$

$$
BAB = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore

$$
A - BAB = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

To test positive semidefiniteness, examine the leading principal minors:

- First leading principal minor: $0$.
- Second leading principal minor (determinant): $\det(A-BAB) = (0)(1) - (1)(1) = -1 < 0$.

A negative determinant means $A - BAB$ has one positive and one negative eigenvalue, so it is **not** positive semidefinite. Equivalently, taking $x = (1,-1)^{\mathsf T}$,

$$
x^{\mathsf T}(A - BAB)x = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix} = -1 < 0.
$$

Hence $BAB \not\le A$ in the quadratic-form sense.

**Conclusion.** The inequality $BAB \le A$ does **not** hold in general. The non-commutativity of $A$ and $B$ is essential: the familiar commutative identity $b^2 a \le a$ (valid when $0\le b\le 1$ and $a\ge 0$ are scalars) does not extend to the matrix setting without commutativity.

### PROOF COMPLETE
